title: Krishna turns to the window
hookLine: Kanakadasa sings outside Udupi and Krishna turns to see him; what a temple is and how to enter
carry: a mandir is god's house; we come as guests
last: A TILAK MARKS THE GOD YOU HONOR.

lines: HE SINGS AT THE BACK WALL.
cards: Udupi, on India's southwest coast, about five hundred years ago. A poet named Kanakadasa, a shepherd's son who sings to Krishna, comes to the great Krishna temple to see his Lord. Because of his caste, he's kept out.

So he goes round to the back wall and sings to Krishna from outside. The story told at Udupi says the image of Krishna turned around to face him, and the wall cracked open into a window, so the two could see each other.
That window is still called Kanaka's window.

teach.b: Notice what the story takes for granted: Krishna is home. That's the teaching today. The Hindi word mandir comes from the Sanskrit mandira: a dwelling, a house.

A temple is understood as a home where God lives, in the murti, the sacred image, which has been ritually installed, like the clay Ganesha you met long ago, and is cared for every day: woken, bathed, dressed, fed, and put to rest at night.
You're not walking into an auditorium.
You're visiting someone's house, and God is the host. That's why everybody first takes off their shoes; there's usually a rack by the door.

Many wash their hands, then ring the bell at the entrance, the ghanta, to say you've arrived. At the heart of the temple is the garbhagriha, the womb-house: small, often dark, lit by lamps, with the main image inside.
In many temples only priests go in; everyone else stands at the threshold, looks, and bows.

teach.h: A MANDIR IS GOD'S HOUSE; WE COME AS GUESTS.
teach.b: There's often no single service: people come and go, though arti times draw a crowd. A few quiet customs: dress modestly, don't point your feet at the shrine, and ask before taking photos.
Many temples welcome visitors of any background; some admit only Hindus. And Kanakadasa's story adds one more thing: the house belongs to God, and God turns toward whoever comes with love.
So if you're nervous at the steps, do what a guest does anywhere. Shoes off, watch, and follow.

how: Visitors to a Hindu temple remove their shoes at the entrance, often wash their hands and ring the bell, then approach the inner shrine to see and bow to the murti, visiting smaller shrines and receiving prasad; most people come and go at any time, with crowds at arti times.

games.q: you're at the temple steps for the first time. if a mandir is God's house, what's the first thing a guest does?
o: walk straight into the inner shrine.
find a seat and wait for a service.
games.why: shoes off, often a hand wash, then the bell. it's God's house, and you're the guest.

practice: Close your eyes and walk in slowly: at the steps, take off your shoes and feel the cool floor, maybe rinse your hands, then ring the bell and listen to it fade.
Walk toward the lamplight, to a small, dim doorway with the image inside, lit by flames, and stop at the threshold. Put your hands together if you'd like, and just stand there, a guest in the house.

wordCard.voice: Mandir. The Hindu temple: a house where God lives and is cared for every day, and where you enter as a guest, shoes off. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit mandira: a dwelling, a house; a temple. Often written मंदिर in Hindi.

carryVoice: Your line: a mandir is God's house; we come as guests. Krishna turned to the window to see his. See you at the threshold.
